distractors.0: Right. Both sides accept writes, so the two halves diverge. A read on either side sees only its own half's version of the world, and when the link heals something has to decide which write wins — last-write-wins, vector clocks, CRDTs, or a human.
distractors.1: This has it backwards. The deployment *kept* availability: both sides go on answering. What it gave up is consistency. Availability would only be the casualty if the system had been configured to refuse service on the minority side — which is what a strictly consistent system does.
distractors.2: Three of six is not a majority. A quorum has to be a strict majority of the whole replica set — four of six here — precisely so that two halves of a partition can never both have one. If each side could form its own quorum, both could commit conflicting writes while believing themselves authoritative, which is the failure quorums exist to prevent.
distractors.3: This is the famous misreading. Partition tolerance is not a design option — the network will partition whether or not you planned for it. So you never get to "choose" P. The real statement is narrower: *while a partition is happening*, you must choose between consistency and availability. The rest of the time you have both, and the trade-off is latency instead.

explanation:
## You chose availability, so you paid in consistency

Both sides keep serving, so neither side stops — availability is intact. But London and Frankfurt are now accepting writes to the same keys with no way to tell each other. The two halves of the dataset diverge, reads return whatever the local half believes, and the divergence has to be reconciled when the link comes back.

That is the whole content of the trade-off, and it is worth stating precisely because the slogan gets it wrong so often.

## "Pick two of three" is the wrong way to remember it

Partition tolerance is not a property you choose. Cables get unplugged, switches reboot, a BGP change blackholes a region. If your answer to a partition is "we do not support that", your answer is that you stop working.

So P is a fact, not an option, and the real theorem is conditional:

> **While a partition is in progress**, a system must choose between answering (and risking staleness) and staying consistent (and refusing some requests).

Martin Kleppmann's *Please stop calling databases CP or AP* is the short version of why the three-way framing misleads. A system is not permanently one letter: it makes this choice per operation, and good systems let you choose per request — which is what a tunable consistency level is.

## Why three of six is not a quorum

Quorums work because **two majorities of the same set must overlap**. With six replicas, a quorum is four. Two disjoint groups of four cannot exist in a set of six, so at most one side of any partition can form one. That is the entire mechanism, and it is why an even split leaves *neither* side able to proceed consistently.

This is also why replica counts are usually odd. Six replicas give you no more partition tolerance than five, and an even split is the one case where a majority system is guaranteed to stall.

## What the other trade-off is

The part CAP leaves out, and which matters far more day to day: even with a perfectly healthy network, a strongly consistent write across London and Frankfurt costs a round trip between them — tens of milliseconds, every time. PACELC adds this explicitly: *if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.*

Partitions are rare. Latency is every single request. Most real architecture decisions are made on the second half of that sentence.
